slides.heading: How Carbon Capture Technology Works
slides.body: The machines pulling CO₂ out of the sky — and what happens next

slides.heading: Why We Need to Capture Carbon
slides.body: Even if we stop all emissions today, CO₂ already in the atmosphere will keep warming the planet for centuries. Carbon capture aims to actively remove that excess, giving humanity a second chance at the 1.5°C target.

slides.heading: Point-Source Capture: Catching It at the Chimney
slides.body: The oldest approach intercepts CO₂ directly from power plants and factories before it enters the air. A chemical solvent — usually an amine — absorbs the gas, then releases it when heated so it can be compressed and stored. This method can cut a single facility's emissions by up to 90%.

slides.heading: Direct Air Capture: Vacuuming the Sky
slides.body: Direct Air Capture (DAC) machines draw in ambient air and pass it over liquid or solid sorbents that bind CO₂. The captured gas is stripped off using heat, yielding a pure CO₂ stream. Climeworks' Mammoth plant in Iceland became the world's largest DAC facility in 2024, pulling 36,000 tonnes per year.

slides.heading: BECCS: Combining Forests with Engineering
slides.body: Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS) grows biomass crops that absorb CO₂ as they grow, burns them for energy, then captures the emissions. The result is energy generation that is carbon-negative — removing more CO₂ than it releases throughout its lifecycle.

slides.heading: What Happens to the Captured CO₂?
slides.body: Captured carbon can be permanently injected into deep geological formations — depleted oil fields or basalt rock — where it mineralizes into stone within years. Alternatively, it becomes a feedstock: making sustainable aviation fuel, concrete, plastics, or even carbonated drinks.

slides.heading: The Cost Challenge
slides.body: DAC currently costs $300–$1,000 per tonne of CO₂ — far above the ~$50 social cost of carbon that makes it economically viable at scale. Researchers are targeting $100 per tonne by 2030 through better sorbents, cheaper renewable energy, and optimized heat cycles.

slides.heading: Scale: The Gigaton Gap
slides.body: The IPCC estimates we need to remove 10 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year by 2050 to meet climate goals. All current carbon capture projects combined remove less than 0.01% of that. Closing this gap requires exponential growth in funding, policy, and engineering talent.

slides.heading: The Controversy: Silver Bullet or Moral Hazard?
slides.body: Critics warn that carbon capture could become an excuse to delay cutting emissions at the source. Others argue it is a necessary complement to renewables, not a replacement. The scientific consensus: capture alone cannot solve climate change, but without it, meeting net-zero targets is nearly impossible.

slides.heading: The Air Is the Frontier
slides.body: Carbon capture is no longer science fiction — it is an engineering and economic challenge. As costs drop and scale grows, the technology that vacuums CO₂ from the sky may become as vital to civilization as the power grid itself.
